Diagrammatic Reasoning with Control as a Constructor, Applications to Quantum Circuits
Noé Delorme, Simon Perdrix

Abstract
Control is a predominant concept in quantum and reversible computational models. It allows to apply or not a transformation on a system, depending on the state of another system. We introduce a general framework for diagrammatic reasoning featuring control as a constructor. To do so, we provide an elementary axiomatisation of control functors, extending the standard formalism of props (symmetric monoidal categories with the natural numbers as objects) to controlled props. As an application, we show that controlled props ease diagrammatic reasoning for quantum circuits by allowing a simple complete set of relations that only involves relations acting on at most three qubits, whereas it is known that in the standard prop setting any complete axiomatisation requires relations acting on arbitrarily many qubits.



1
Introduction

Diagrammatic reasoning has been very successful in the recent years in various domains including quantum computing
[
12
,
19
,
16
,
4
,
1
,
10
]
, linear algebra
[
24
,
7
]
, control theory
[
6
,
5
]
, natural language processing
[
11
,
25
]
and symbolic dynamics
[
18
]
to cite a few. The natural mathematical framework for diagrammatic reasoning is that of symmetric monoidal categories, and more precisely, props. This formalism allows to represent processes and how they interact in space-time via sequential and parallel compositions. To do so, we can define graphical languages as generators and relations, allowing to reason on string diagrams rather than on their interpretations, which can be less intuitive and/or significantly larger – such as matrices whose dimensions grow exponentially with the number of inputs and outputs in the quantum case.

Control is a central concept in quantum and reversible computational models. Roughly speaking, a transformation can be conditioned on an additional system such that, depending on its state, the transformation is either applied or not. For instance, controlling a NOT gate yields the well-known CNOT gate, and adding another control leads to the Toffoli gate. Notice, that various quantum programming languages
[
15
,
14
,
22
,
3
,
13
]
provide primitives that allow to control gates or even circuits.

In this paper, we aim at formalising the notion of control as a constructor in graphical languages, i.e. as a functor in a prop: every diagram
f
with
n
inputs and
n
outputs yields a new diagram
\textup{{C}}(f)
with
1+n
inputs and
1+n
outputs, which represents its controlled version (notice that our control only applies to diagrams with equal numbers of input and outputs). A controlled prop is then defined as a prop equipped with a control functor. Similarly to props, controlled props can be used to define graphical languages as generators and relations.

In these settings, the control distributes over composition: given two composable diagrams
f
and
g
, we have that
\textup{{C}}(g\circ f)=\textup{{C}}(g)\circ\textup{{C}}(f)
. This reflects the intuition that controlling a sequence of operations is equivalent to sequentially controlling each operation. As control does not distribute over parallel composition (
\textup{{C}}(f\otimes g)\neq\textup{{C}}(f)\otimes\textup{{C}}(g)
, since the latter acts on one more wire), we provide a simple axiomatisation that allows in particular to define the control of a parallel composition of two diagrams. Additionally, our formalism satisfies a context rule saying that if an equation
f=g
is derivable, so is its control version
\textup{{C}}(f)=\textup{{C}}(g)
. This follows directly from the definition of control as a constructor.

Control functors also allow to state the fondamental conjugation law, which is a cornerstone when dealing with reversing and control. Given an arbitrary
f
and a reversible
g
– which inverse is denoted
g^{\dagger}
– one can conjugate
f
by
g
, leading to the pattern
g^{\dagger}\circ f\circ g
. This pattern is widely used in algorithm design, e.g. for a basis change, for ancillary qubit preparation and liberation, or for oracle implementation. Controlling such a pattern can be reduced to controlling only
f
, leading to the following conjugation law.

An important motivation for our framework comes from quantum computing, where control is extensively used to conditionally apply a gate according to the state of one or multiple control qubits. Beyond controlling individual gates, quantum algorithms often rely on conditioning entire subcircuits which can be expressed in the formalism of controlled props where quantum circuits are represented as string diagrams.

Complete sets of relations for quantum circuits have been established in earlier works using the formalism of props
[
10
,
9
,
8
]
. These complete equational theories do not rely on the control as a constructor, but point out however the pivotal role of controlled operations in diagrammatic reasoning, and motivates the introduction of controlled props. As our main application in this present paper, we define the controllable quantum circuits and give a complete set of relations for it. This fairly natural and simple complete set of relations, depicted in
Figure

1
, is made of
4
basic equations (
Equations

1
,
2
,
3
and
4
), together with the standard Euler decomposition
Equation

5
, and 4 instances of the conjugation law (
Equations

6
,
7
,
8
and
9
).

(9)

Figure 1
:
Complete set of relations for the graphical language of controllable quantum circuits using the controlled prop formalism. Note that this presentation uses some shorthand notations to align with usual gate choices in quantum computing. Especially, the Z-rotation gates are in fact controlled global phases. The explicit presentation is depicted in
Figure

5
.

Remarkably, in the complete set of relations we introduce for controllable quantum circuits, all relations involve circuits acting on at most three qubits, whereas, it has been shown in
[
8
]
that any complete set of relations for (unitary) quantum circuits, defined as a prop, requires at least one relation involving circuits acting on
n
wires for any
n\in\mathbb{N}
. Hence, using controlled props allow to circumvent the unboundedness issue of props, demonstrating the formalism of controlled props is particularly appropriate for quantum circuit reasoning.

Using control as a constructor also impacts the generators of the graphical languages. As a prop, the generators of the quantum circuits are the so called universal gate sets, for instance Z-rotation gates, the Hadamard gate, the CNOT gate together with the global phases are a common choice. It turns out that we can consider much simpler generators in the context of controlled props. This is because a Z-rotation gate is nothing but a controlled global phase gate. Similarly, as soon as we have the NOT gate, we have by construction the CNOT gate. Hence, quantum circuits, as a controlled prop, can be generated by the global phases and the Hadamard gate only.

Related work.

In graphical languages, control is a central notion that has been used in various contexts, but not as a constructor. For quantum circuits, the completeness procedure is based on a back and forth translation with optical circuits
[
10
]
. The encoding of optical circuits into quantum circuits extensively relies on controlled operations, and their basic algebra. In this context, controlled operations are considered as shorthand notations, as they can be decomposed into generators. In the ZX-calculus, controlled diagrams have also been extensively used in particular for defining normal forms
[
20
]
, notice that the expressivity of the language allows to define control in a slightly difference way, allowing the control of arbitrary diagram (not necessarily with the same number of inputs and outputs). Again in this context, controlled operations are considered as shorthand notations. Notice that controlled states and diagrams have also received some interests in the ZXW-calculus
[
2
]
. A very interesting approach consists in extending the quantum circuit model by allowing a new kind of composition which graphically consists in vertically connecting two gates, the behaviour of the new composed gates depends on the hamiltonians of the original ones. This work in progress allows, for instance, to represent a CNOT by connecting a Z gate to a X gate
[
23
]
. Additionally, various quantum programming languages (especially circuit description languages) allows for control of quantum circuits. In particular, Quipper supports control and a
withcompute
primitive, which consists in conjugating a circuit with another. These features have been semantically formalised using controllable categories
[
14
]
which involving control functions which are not necessarily functors. The goal of controllable categories is to provide a categorical model for a high level quantum programming language, while controlled props aim to formalize control in graphical languages, with much less features. Another quantum programming language introduced very recently in
[
17
]
allows any arbitrary unitaries to be generated from some simple global phases combined with a quantum analogue of
if let
primitive, which can be embedded in our formalism (see
Section

5.2
).

Structure of the paper.
In
Section

2
, we fix the notations and recall the usual notions used to define a graphical language in the prop formalism. In
Section

3
, we introduce the controlled prop formalism and its underlying notion of conjugation. In
Section

4
, we define controllable quantum circuits (as a controlled prop), prove that the conjugation holds, and give a complete set of relations for it. In
Section

5
, we extend and generalise the framework of controlled prop in several ways. Especially, we review some notable properties that multiple coexisting control functors may satisfy, as well as generalising control functors for arbitrary symmetric monoidal categories. In
Section

6
, we provide our concluding remarks. Additionally, the paper contains three appendicies containing detailed proofs of the main results.

2
Background

2.1
Symmetric monoidal categories

In a nutshell, a
strict symmetric monoidal category
(SMC)
C
consists in a collection of objects
\mathcal{O}(\textbf{{C}})
and for any objects
A,B\in\mathcal{O}(\textbf{{C}})
, a collection of morphisms
\textbf{{C}}(A,B)
, together with two composition operators
\circ
and
\otimes
respectively called
sequential composition
and
parallel composition
(or
tensor product
). The objects are freely generated by
\otimes
such that
(A\otimes B)\otimes C=A\otimes(B\otimes C)
and there is a neutral object
I
such that
A\otimes I=A=I\otimes A
. We write
f:A\to B
when
f
is a morphism in
\textbf{{C}}(A,B)
, moreover
A
and
B
are respectively called the
domain
and
codomain
of
f
. For each pair of morphisms
f:A\to B
,
g:B\to C
, there is a morphism
g\circ f:A\to C
. For each pair of morphisms
f:A\to B
,
g:C\to D
, there is a morphism
f\otimes g:A\otimes C\to B\otimes D
. For each
A\in\mathcal{O}(\textbf{{C}})
there is an identity morphism
\textup{id}_{A}
and for each
A,B\in\mathcal{O}(\textbf{{C}})
there is a permutation morphism
\sigma_{A,B}
. Finally, the morphisms in a SMC have to satisfy the
coherence laws
depicted in
Figure

2
. SMCs have a nice representation as string diagrams where objects are depicted as wires and morphism as boxes. Unlike morphisms, where both compositions are in the same dimension, strings diagrams takes advantage of a second dimension by drawing the parallel compositions vertically. Many morphism equivalences are then trivialised in the graphical representation.

\textup{id}_{A}:A\to A

\sigma_{A,B}:A\otimes B\to B\otimes A

g\circ f:A\to C

f\otimes g:A\otimes C\to B\otimes D

(19)

Figure 2
:
Coherence laws of symmetric monoidal categories.

Given two categories
C
and
D
, a
functor

F:\textbf{{C}}\to\textbf{{D}}
is a map which assigns to each object
A\in\mathcal{O}(\textbf{{C}})
an object
F(A)\in\mathcal{O}(\textbf{{D}})
, and to each morphism
f\in\textbf{{C}}(A,B)
a morphism
F(f)\in\textbf{{D}}(F(A),F(B))
while preserving the compositional structure, that is
F(\textup{id}_{A})=\textup{id}_{F(A)}
and
F(g\circ f)=F(g)\circ F(f)
whenever
g\circ f
is defined. We say that
F
is
monoidal
when it also preserves the tensor product, that is
F(I)=I
,
F(A\otimes B)=F(A)\otimes F(B)
, and
F(f\otimes g)=F(f)\otimes F(g)
. We say that
F
is
symmetric
when it also preserves the permutation morphisms, that is
F(\sigma_{A,B})=\sigma_{F(A),F(B)}
.

Example 1
.

The Hilbert spaces of finite dimension form a SMC
FdHilb
whose objects are
\mathbb{C}^{n}
where
\mathbb{C}^{n}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{m}
is identified to
\mathbb{C}^{nm}
when
n,m\in\mathbb{N}
and whose morphisms are linear maps with the usual tensor product as monoidal product (with
\mathbb{C}
as neutral object). The identities are the linear maps of the form
\sum_{x}\left|x\right\rangle\!\left\langle x\right|
and the permutations are the linear maps of the form
\sum_{x,y}\left|y,x\right\rangle\!\left\langle x,y\right|
. One can check that all coherence laws (see
Figure

2
) are satisfied.
FdHilb
and its sub-categories will be our running example throughout the paper.

2.2
Graphical languages

We are particularily interested in a subclass of SMCs that are used to model graphical languages, namely
prop
s (which stands for
products and permutations categories
). A prop
P
is a SMC whose objects are generated by a single object
A
and the tensor product
\otimes
, or equivalentely, whose objects are the natural numbers with addition as tensor product (just identify the object
A^{\otimes n}
with
n\in\mathbb{N}
where
A^{\otimes 0}\coloneqq I
and
A^{\otimes n+1}\coloneqq A^{\otimes n}\otimes A
). A diagram with
n
inputs and
m
outputs represents a morphism
f\in\textbf{{P}}(n,m)
. Endomorphisms, i.e. morphisms with equal domain and codomain, form a sub-prop denoted
\textbf{{P}}_{\textup{endo}}
.

Example 2
.

Given
d\in\mathbb{N}
, let
\textbf{{FdHilb}}_{\bm{d}}
be the sub-category of
FdHilb
(defined in
Example

1
) whose objects are of the form
\mathbb{C}^{d^{n}}
for some
n\in\mathbb{N}
. Then,
\textbf{{FdHilb}}_{\bm{d}}
form a prop as
\mathbb{C}^{d}
generates all other objects with the tensor product
\otimes
. Moreover, the category
Qubit
whose morphisms are the ones of
\textbf{{FdHilb}}_{\bm{2}}
restained to unitary maps is a sub-prop of
\textbf{{FdHilb}}_{\bm{2}}
. Notice that
\textbf{{Qubit}}_{\textup{endo}}
and
Qubit
are the same as unitaries have the same number of inputs and outputs.

Graphical languages can be defined as props by generators and relations. That is, the diagrams are compositions of the generators quotiented by a set of relations as well as the coherence laws depicted in
Figure

2
. The relations can be seen as rewrite rules used to transform diagrams into equivalent ones. Given a graphical language
P
, we write
\textbf{{P}}\vdash D_{1}=D_{2}
when the diagram
D_{1}
can be transformed into
D_{2}
using its relations and the coherence laws.

When defining a graphical languages
P
as a prop, we often want to interpret the diagrams. To do so, we define an interpretation (symmetric monoidal) functor
\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket:\textbf{{P}}\to\textbf{{S}}
. An important property of the graphical language is
soundness
, which means that every equivalences that can be derived in
P
respects
\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket
. The cornerstone is to prove the reverse which is known as
completeness
.
Formally, we say that the graphical language
P
is sound if
\textbf{{P}}\vdash D_{1}=D_{2}
implies
\llbracket D_{1}\rrbracket=\llbracket D_{2}\rrbracket
for any
D_{1},D_{2}\in\textbf{{P}}(n,m)
, and that it is complete if
\llbracket D_{1}\rrbracket=\llbracket D_{2}\rrbracket
implies
\textbf{{P}}\vdash D_{1}=D_{2}
for any
D_{1},D_{2}\in\textbf{{P}}(n,m)
.

Additionally, a dagger prop
P
is a prop equipped with a
dagger
functor
(\cdot)^{\dagger}:\textbf{{P}}\to\textbf{{P}}
, which is an identity-on-object involutive contravariant monoidal functor, meaning that every morphism
f:n\to m
has a dagger
f^{\dagger}:m\to n
satisfying
(g\circ f)^{\dagger}=f^{\dagger}\circ g^{\dagger}
,
(f\otimes g)^{\dagger}=f^{\dagger}\otimes g^{\dagger}
and
f^{\dagger\dagger}=f
. Moreover
\sigma_{n,m}^{\dagger}=\sigma_{m,n}
has to be satisfied for any
n,m\in\mathbb{N}
. Throughout the paper, we denote the dagger functor of a dagger prop by
(\cdot)^{\dagger}
unless a different notation is specified.

Example 3
.

\textbf{{FdHilb}}_{\bm{d}}
(defined in
Example

2
) form a dagger prop where the dagger is the usual adjoint.

3
Control and conjugation

In this section, we formalise the notion of control as a constructor in a prop. Formally, this is achieved by equipping a prop with a control functor that satisfies some coherence laws.

Definition 1

(control functor)
.

Given a prop
P
, a
control functor

\textup{{C}}:\textbf{{P}}_{\textup{endo}}\to\textbf{{P}}_{\textup{endo}}
is a (non-monoidal) functor mapping any object
n\in\mathbb{N}
to the object
1+n
and mapping any morphism
f:n\to n
to a morphism
\textup{{C}}(f):1+n\to 1+n
while satisfying the coherence laws depicted in
Figure

3
.

\begin{array}[]{ccc}\textup{{C}}(f\otimes\textup{id}_{k})&=&\textup{{C}}(f)\otimes\textup{id}_{k}\\[3.99994pt]

nested application of the control functor
C
from
f
. Formally,
\textup{{C}}^{0}(f)\coloneqq f

. Also, the coherence laws of prop (

Notice that the fact that
C
is a functor implies
\textup{{C}}(g\circ f)=\textup{{C}}(g)\circ\textup{{C}}(f)
whenever
g\circ f
is defined, and the fact that
\textup{{C}}(n)=1+n
implies that
\textup{{C}}(\textup{id}_{n})=\textup{id}_{1+n}
. However,
C
is not monoidal as
\textup{{C}}(f\otimes g)\neq\textup{{C}}(f)\otimes\textup{{C}}(g)
in general. Rather, we have the following.

Example 4
.

In
\textbf{{FdHilb}}_{\bm{2}}
, the standard notion of control is to apply a map
U:\mathbb{C}^{2^{n}}\to\mathbb{C}^{2^{n}}
on the targeted system when the control qubit is in the state
\left|1\right\rangle
, and to apply the identity
I_{2^{n}}
when the control qubit is in the state
\left|0\right\rangle
. This can be embedded as the control functor defined as follows.

\textup{{C}}_{1}:U\mapsto\left|0\right\rangle\!\left\langle 0\right|\otimes I_{2^{n}}+\left|1\right\rangle\!\left\langle 1\right|\otimes U

However, this is not the only control functor. For instance,
\textup{{C}}_{0}:U\mapsto\left|0\right\rangle\!\left\langle 0\right|\otimes U+\left|1\right\rangle\!\left\langle 1\right|\otimes I_{2^{n}}
or
\textup{{C}}_{-}:U\mapsto\left|+\right\rangle\!\left\langle+\right|\otimes I_{2^{n}}+\left|-\right\rangle\!\left\langle-\right|\otimes U
(where
\left|+\right\rangle\coloneqq\nicefrac{{1}}{{\sqrt{2}}}(\left|0\right\rangle+\left|1\right\rangle)
and
\left|-\right\rangle\coloneqq\nicefrac{{1}}{{\sqrt{2}}}(\left|0\right\rangle-\left|1\right\rangle)
) are also control functors in
\textbf{{FdHilb}}_{\bm{2}}
. In higher dimensions,
\textbf{{FdHilb}}_{\bm{d}}
admit a control functor

\textstyle\textup{{C}}_{k}:U\mapsto\left|k\right\rangle\!\left\langle k\right|\otimes U+\sum_{\ell\neq k}\left|\ell\right\rangle\!\left\langle\ell\right|\otimes I_{d^{n}}

for any natural number
0\leq k<d
. Notice however that the map
U\mapsto\sum_{k}\left|k\right\rangle\!\left\langle k\right|\otimes U^{k}
is not a control functor as it fails to be functorial in general when
d>2
.

We now focus on props equipped with a single control functor, that we call
controlled props
, the general case of props with several control functors is described in
Section

5.2
. Notice that a single control functor already offers a rich structure as other control functors can be obtained by applying some gates on the control wire. For instance in
\textbf{{FdHilb}}_{\bm{2}}
one can recover the various examples described in
Example

4
by applying a NOT or Hadamard gate on the control qubit.

Definition 2

(controlled prop)
.

A
controlled prop
is a prop equipped with a control functor.

Throughout the paper, we denote the control functor of a controlled prop by
C
, unless a different notation is specified. For instance,
\textbf{{FdHilb}}_{\bm{2}}
is a controlled prop with
U\mapsto\left|0\right\rangle\!\left\langle 0\right|\otimes I_{2^{n}}+\left|1\right\rangle\!\left\langle 1\right|\otimes U
as control functor.

Similarly to props, controlled props can be used to define graphical languages. The only difference is that for any diagram
f\in\textbf{{P}}(n,n)
, we also have a diagram
\textup{{C}}(f)\in\textbf{{P}}(1+n,1+n)
. Moreover, a prop may have both dagger and control functors. This is particularily of intereset as it allows to state the fondamental conjugation law.

Definition 3

(dagger controlled prop)
.

A
dagger controlled prop

P
is both a dagger prop and a controlled prop that satisfies
(\textup{{C}}(f))^{\dagger}=\textup{{C}}(f^{\dagger})
for any
f\in\textbf{{P}}(n,n)
.

Definition 4

(conjugation)
.

A dagger controlled prop is said to be
conjugated
when
Equation

23
is satisfied for any
f:m\to m
and
g:n\to m
such that
g
is an isometry, i.e.
g^{\dagger}\circ g=\textup{id}_{n}
.

\begin{array}[]{ccc}\textup{{C}}(g^{\dagger}\circ f\circ g)&=&(\textup{id}_{1}\otimes g^{\dagger})\circ\textup{{C}}(f)\circ(\textup{id}_{1}\otimes g)\\[3.99994pt]

}}\end{array}

(23)

Equation

23
is know as the
conjugation law
, and expresses that controlling a conjugated operation is equivalent to conjugating a controlled operation. Intuitively, if you apply a gate
f
“in the middle” of a pattern
g^{\dagger}\circ f\circ g
, then controlling the entire pattern is the same as just controlling the gate
f
and wrapping the control around with
g
and
g^{\dagger}
.

This law is particularly important in algorithm design where the pattern
g^{\dagger}\circ f\circ g
is often used to prepare and uncompute ancillary bits (or qubits). This law can be used as much as possible in some compilation processes to minimize the scope of control.

Example 5
.

\textbf{{FdHilb}}_{\bm{2}}
with the control functor
U\mapsto\left|0\right\rangle\!\left\langle 0\right|\otimes I_{2^{n}}+\left|1\right\rangle\!\left\langle 1\right|\otimes U
form a dagger controlled prop and is conjugated. The same holds for its restriction
Qubit
.

In
Appendix

A
, we give a sufficient condition for the conjugation law to hold in the context of a unitary dagger controlled prop, i.e. when
\textbf{{P}}\vdash f^{\dagger}\circ f=\textup{id}_{n}=f\circ f^{\dagger}
for any
f\in\textbf{{P}}(n,n)
. Intuitively, in these settings, proving the conjugation law for basic gates is enough to ensure that is holds for any
f
and
g
. This gives a procedure to show that a controlled prop is conjugated.

4
Quantum circuits

In the section, we apply the controlled prop formalism to quantum circuits and compare it to the prop formalism.
Section

4.1
introduces the graphical language of
vanilla quantum circuits
as a prop and recall the already know complete set of relations for it.
Section

4.2
introduces the graphical langage of
controllable quantum circuits
as a controlled prop and give a complete set of relations for it.

(33)

Figure 4
:
Relations
\mathcal{R}_{\textup{vanilla}}
for the graphical language of vanilla quantum circuits
QC
. The circuit
\lambda^{n}(\alpha)
is defined in
Section

4.1
and
\mathcal{R}_{\textup{vanilla}}
contains an instance of
Equation

33
for any number of qubits
n\geq 3
.

Quantum circuits are interpreted by the symmetric monoidal functor
\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}
as unitary maps in
Qubit
. Notice that the fact that
\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}
is a symmetric monoidal functor gives directly the interpretation of composition of circuits by
\llbracket C_{2}\circ C_{1}\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}\coloneqq\llbracket C_{2}\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}\circ\llbracket C_{1}\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}
and
\llbracket C_{1}\otimes C_{2}\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}\coloneqq\llbracket C_{1}\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}\otimes\llbracket C_{2}\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}
. Similarly, for the identities and permutations we have
\llbracket\textup{id}_{n}\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}\coloneqq\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\left|x\right\rangle\!\left\langle x\right|
and
\llbracket\sigma_{n,m}\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}\coloneqq\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n},y\in\{0,1\}^{m}}\left|y,x\right\rangle\!\left\langle x,y\right|
.

(standard interpretation)
.

}}\right\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}\coloneqq\sum_{x,y\in\{0,1\}}\left|x,x\oplus y\right\rangle\!\left\langle x,y\right|

This assigns a unitary to all circuits in
QC
. Conversaly, it is well-know that any unitary can be expressed as a circuit in
QC
. This property is know as
universality
and ensures that the graphical language captures all the quantum evolutions.

Proposition 1

(universality)
.

QC
is universal for
Qubit
, i.e. for any unitary
U\in\textbf{{Qubit}}(n,n)
there exists a circuit
C\in\textbf{{QC}}(n,n)
such that
\llbracket C\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}=U
.

In particular, we can implement any controlled operation by composing basic gates. For instance, the multi-controlled Z-rotations can be implemented for any
\alpha\in\mathbb{R}
and
n\in\mathbb{N}
by the following circuit
\lambda^{n}(\alpha)\in\textbf{{QC}}(n,n)
.

Notice that, once unfolded, the circuit
\lambda^{n}(\alpha)
is huge as it contains exponentially many

Z(\nicefrac{{\alpha}}{{2^{n-1}}})

gates. Moreover, we can check that the standard interpretation (see
Definition

6
) of the circuit
\lambda^{n}(\alpha)
is the desired Z-rotations with parameter
\alpha
and controlled by the first
n-1
qubits.

\textstyle\llbracket\lambda^{n}(\alpha)\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}=e^{i\alpha}\left|1\dots 1\right\rangle\!\left\langle 1\dots 1\right|+\sum_{x\neq 1\dots 1}\left|x\right\rangle\!\left\langle x\right|

It as been shown in
[
8
]
that the graphical language
QC
is complete. Meaning that any equivalent (i.e. with the same standard interpretation) circuits
C_{1},C_{2}
can be transformed one into the other using the relations in
\mathcal{R}_{\textup{vanilla}}
together with the coherence laws.

Theorem 1

(
[
8
]
)
.

The graphical language
QC
is complete.

All the relations in
\mathcal{R}_{\textup{vanilla}}
are simple and commonly used in the litterature. Surely the most powerful relation is
Equation

28
.

This relation follows from the well-know Euler’s decomposition which states that any unitary can be decomposed, up to a global phase, into basic X- and Z-rotations. The angles
\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}
are arbitrary in
\mathbb{R}
whereas the angles
\beta_{0},\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3}
are restricted to
[0,2\pi)
and are computed by explicit functions as follows using the intermediate complex numbers
u,v\in\mathbb{C}
.

\displaystyle u\coloneqq-\sin\left(\nicefrac{{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}}{{2}}\right)+i\cos\left(\nicefrac{{\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}}}{{2}}\right)\hskip 30.00005ptv\coloneqq\cos\left(\nicefrac{{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}}{{2}}\right)-i\sin\left(\nicefrac{{\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}}}{{2}}\right)

\beta_{1}

\beta_{2}

\beta_{3}

if
v=0

2\arg(u)

0

0

if
u=0

2\arg(v)

\pi

0

otherwise

\arg(u)+\arg(v)

2\arg\left(i+\left\lvert\nicefrac{{u}}{{v}}\right\rvert\right)

\arg(u)-\arg(v)

and

\beta_{0}\coloneqq\frac{(\pi+\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}-\beta_{3})}{2}

Moreover, it as been shown in
[
8
]
that every relation of
\mathcal{R}_{\textup{vanilla}}
is necessary. This means that none can be removed without loosing completeness. Notice that there is an instance of
Equation

33
for any number of qubits
n\geq 3
. All such instances are necessary. More generally, any set of relations yielding a complete and universal graphical language (defined as a prop) for unitary maps requires at least one relation acting on
n
qubits for all
n\in\mathbb{N}
. As we will see in the following section, this is not true anymore using the controlled prop formalism.

4.2
Controllable quantum circuits

Using the controlled prop formalism, we can use much simpler gate sets to define quantum circuits. This is because a Z-rotation gate can be seen as a controlled global phase gate, and a CNOT gate can be seen as controlled NOT gate. In fact, we can just take the global phases together with the Hadamard gate as gate set and still capture all unitaries in
Qubit
.

Definition 7

(controllable quantum circuits)
.

The
controllable quantum circuits
are defined as the control prop
CQC
defined by the following generators where
\alpha\in\mathbb{R}
and the relations
\mathcal{R}_{\textup{control}}
depicted in
Figure

5
.

(44)

Figure 5
:
Relations
\mathcal{R}_{\textup{control}}
for the graphical language of controllable quantum circuits
CQC
.

We extend the standard interpretation of vanilla quantum circuits (see
Definition

6
) to embed the control. This is achieved with the following symmetric monoidal functor
\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket_{\textup{c}}
.

Definition 8

(standard interpretation)
.

The standard interpretation
\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket_{\textup{c}}:\textbf{{CQC}}\to\textbf{{Qubit}}
of controllable quantum circuits is the symmetric monoidal functor defined as follows.

Lemma 1
.

\textbf{{CQC}}\vdash C^{\dagger}\circ C=\textup{id}_{n}=C\circ C^{\dagger}
for any
C\in\textbf{{CQC}}(n,n)
.

Proof.

By structural induction on
C
using
(C_{2}\circ C_{1})^{\dagger}\circ(C_{2}\circ C_{1})=C_{1}^{\dagger}\circ C_{2}^{\dagger}\circ C_{2}\circ C_{1}=C_{1}^{\dagger}\circ C_{1}=\textup{id}_{n}
,
(C_{1}\otimes C_{2})^{\dagger}\circ(C_{1}\otimes C_{2})=(C_{1}^{\dagger}\otimes C_{2}^{\dagger})\circ(C_{1}\otimes C_{2})=(C_{1}^{\dagger}\circ C_{1})\otimes(C_{2}^{\dagger}\circ C_{2})=\textup{id}_{n}\otimes\textup{id}_{m}=\textup{id}_{n+m}
and
(\textup{{C}}(C))^{\dagger}\circ\textup{{C}}(C)=\textup{{C}}(C^{\dagger})\circ\textup{{C}}(C)=\textup{{C}}(C^{\dagger}\circ C)=\textup{{C}}(\textup{id}_{n})=\textup{id}_{n+1}
. The base case
C=\scalebox{0.90}{{

∎

The following three equations reduce the number of controls of a gate at the cost of introducing other gates with less controls. This is particularily useful to establish the correpondance with the vanilla quantum circuits. Indeed, we can transform any controllable quantum circuit into one that contains only gates controlled by up to two qubits, and all such gates correspond to a certain vanilla quantum circuit.

These equations are proved in
Appendix

B
and are used to prove the conjugation law for controllable quantum circuits in the following proposition.

Proposition 2
.

CQC
is conjugated.

Proof.

Appendix

A
gives a sufficient condition for the conjugation law to hold in the case of a dagger controlled prop
P
that contains only endomorphisms and such that
\textbf{{P}}\vdash C\circ C^{\dagger}=\textup{id}_{n}=C^{\dagger}\circ C
for any
C\in\textbf{{P}}(n,n)
. It turns out that
CQC
satisfies these conditions (see
Lemma

1
). The idea is to transform any morphism
C
into a morphism
C^{\prime}
made of compositions of some gates in a chosen set
\mathcal{G}
and such that
C^{\prime}
has the form

\displaystyle(\textup{id}_{p_{\ell}}\otimes x_{\ell}\otimes\textup{id}_{q_{\ell}})\circ(\textup{id}_{p_{\ell-1}}\otimes x_{\ell-1}\otimes\textup{id}_{q_{\ell-1}})\circ\dots\circ(\textup{id}_{p_{1}}\otimes x_{1}\otimes\textup{id}_{q_{1}})

where
x_{k}
is one of the gate of
\mathcal{G}
. Intuitively,
C^{\prime}
is a sequencial composition of layers containing only one gate. In the case of
CQC
,
Equations

45
,
46
and
47
(together with
Equation

38
) allow to transform any circuit into one that contains only the following gates.

\alpha

\alpha

\pi

H

Then, roughly speaking, the sufficient condition states that this is enough to prove the conjugation law for individual layers to ensure that it is provable for all circuits. The details are given in
Appendix

B
.
∎

and

4.1

Intuitively,
\mu^{n}(\alpha)
is an implementation of the Z-rotation gate with parameter
\alpha
and controlled by
n-1
first qubits. It is provably equivalent to directly control a

\alpha

gate.

.

∎

We are now ready to prove completeness for controllable quantum circuits by reducing it to the completeness of vanilla quantum circuits (see
Theorem

1
).

Theorem 2

(completeness)
.

The graphical language
CQC
is complete.

Proof.

Rougly speaking, we use the fact that
QC
is complete by translating the proofs from
QC
to
CQC
. To do so, we define an encoding map
E:\textbf{{CQC}}\to\textbf{{QC}}
and a decoding map
D:\textbf{{QC}}\to\textbf{{CQC}}
satisfying
\llbracket E(C)\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}=\llbracket C\rrbracket_{\textup{c}}
for any
C\in\textbf{{CQC}}(n,n)
and
\llbracket D(C)\rrbracket_{\textup{c}}=\llbracket C\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}
for any
C\in\textbf{{QC}}(n,n)
. Then, given
C_{1},C_{2}\in\textbf{{CQC}}(n,n)
such that
\llbracket C_{1}\rrbracket_{\textup{c}}=\llbracket C_{2}\rrbracket_{\textup{c}}
. By competeness (see
Theorem

1
)
\textbf{{QC}}\vdash E(C_{1})=E(C_{2})
, and we can decode this proof using
D
to get a proof of
\textbf{{CQC}}\vdash D(E(C_{1}))=D(E(C_{2}))
. This uses in particular the fact that
\textbf{{CQC}}\vdash D(\lambda^{n}(\alpha))=\mu^{n}(\alpha)
. To conclude, we also need to show that
\textbf{{CQC}}\vdash D(E(C))=C
for any
C\in\textbf{{CQC}}(n,n)
. To simplify the proof, this process is not directly applied to
CQC
, but to a subclass of circuits
\textbf{{CQC}}|_{\mathcal{G}}
. The details are given in
Appendix

C
.
∎

It is remarkable that
\mathcal{R}_{\textup{control}}
only contains relations acting on at most three qubits, whereas this was not possible in the prop formalism. This is mainly possible thanks to the context rule saying that if
\textbf{{CQC}}\vdash C_{1}=C_{2}
then
\textbf{{CQC}}\vdash\textup{{C}}(C_{1})=\textup{{C}}(C_{2})
which comes at free cost by definition of the control as a constructor.

5
Extensions and generalisations

In this section we extend and generalise the formalism of controlled prop in several ways.

5.1
Points

A natural extension for control functor is the notion of
points
. Intuitively, the points of a control functor are two specific morphisms
\textup{{true}},\textup{{false}}:0\to 1
that respectively fires and annihilates the controlled operation when they are plugged to the control wire.

Definition 9
.

A control functor
has points
if there exist two morphisms
\textup{{true}},\textup{{false}}:0\to 1
such that the following equations are satisfied for any
f:n\to n
.

\textup{{C}}(f)\circ(\textup{{true}}\otimes\textup{id}_{n})=\textup{{true}}\otimes f\hskip 50.00008pt\textup{{C}}(f)\circ(\textup{{false}}\otimes\textup{id}_{n})=\textup{{false}}\otimes\textup{id}_{n}

Example 6
.

In
\textbf{{FdHilb}}_{\bm{2}}
, the points of the control functor
U\mapsto\left|0\right\rangle\!\left\langle 0\right|\otimes I_{2^{n}}+\left|1\right\rangle\!\left\langle 1\right|\otimes U
are
\left|1\right\rangle
and
\left|0\right\rangle
.

Notice however that points do not necessarily exist, in particular when all morphisms of the prop are endomorphisms, like in
CQC
and
Qubit
.

5.2
Polycontrolled props

Throughout the paper, we focused on props that are equipped with a single control functor. This is natural to consider
polycontrolled props
, i.e. props that have multiple control functors.
In the following, we review some notable properties that multiple coexisting control functors may satisfy.

Definition 10

(compatibility)
.

Given a polycontrolled prop
P
with control functors
\textup{{C}}_{1}
and
\textup{{C}}_{2}
, we say that
\textup{{C}}_{1}
and
\textup{{C}}_{2}
are
compatible
if the following equation is satisfied for any
f\in\textbf{{P}}(n,n)
.

\begin{array}[]{ccc}\textup{{C}}_{1}(\textup{{C}}_{2}(f))\circ(\sigma_{1,1}\otimes\textup{id}_{n})&=&(\sigma_{1,1}\otimes\textup{id}_{n})\circ\textup{{C}}_{2}(\textup{{C}}_{1}(f))\\[3.99994pt]

(50)

Example 7
.

In
\textbf{{FdHilb}}_{\bm{2}}
(see
Example

4
),
\textup{{C}}_{1}
is compatible with
\textup{{C}}_{0}
because each control can be obtained by conjugating the control wire of the other control with a NOT gate that slides through the swaps.
However,
\textup{{C}}_{1}
is not compatible with the control functor
\textup{{C}}_{\sharp}:U\mapsto I_{2}\otimes X_{n}UX_{n}
where
U
acts on
n
qubits and where
X_{n}
applies NOT gates to
n
qubits in parallel. Intuitively,
\textup{{C}}_{\sharp}
is independent of the control qubit and always conjugate the target by a series of NOT gates in parallel.

Definition 11

(commutativity)
.

Given a polycontrolled prop
P
with control functors
\textup{{C}}_{1}
and
\textup{{C}}_{2}
, we say that
\textup{{C}}_{1}
and
\textup{{C}}_{2}

commute
if the following equation is satisfied for any
f,g\in\textbf{{P}}(n,n)
.

\begin{array}[]{ccc}\textup{{C}}_{2}(g)\circ\textup{{C}}_{1}(f)&=&\textup{{C}}_{1}(f)\circ\textup{{C}}_{2}(g)\\[3.99994pt]

Example 8
.

In
\textbf{{FdHilb}}_{\bm{2}}
(see

),

commutes with

whereas it does not commute with

.

Definition 12

(exhausivity)
.

Given a polycontrolled prop
P
with a family of
\ell
commuting control functors
(\textup{{C}}_{k})_{k\in[\ell]}
, we say that the family is exhaustive if the following equation is satisfied for any
f\in\textbf{{P}}(n,n)
.

\begin{array}[]{ccc}\textup{{C}}_{\ell}(f)\circ\ldots\circ\textup{{C}}_{1}(f)&=&\textup{id}_{1}\otimes f\\[3.99994pt]

(52)

Example 9
.

In
\textbf{{FdHilb}}_{\bm{d}}
(see
Example

4
), the family of control functors
(\textup{{C}}_{k})_{0\leq k<d}
is exhausitive. Intuitively, each controlled operation
\textup{{C}}_{k}(f)
fires
f
if the control qubit is in the state
\left|k\right\rangle
. Thus, if we apply all these controlled operations sequentially, then
f
is always fired exactly once.

While controllable quantum circuits are defined using two generators and one control functor, we could also define them using one generator and two control functors. This idea as first been explained in
[
17
]
, and can be expressed in the controlled prop formalism as folows: if we only have global phases

\alpha

for any
\alpha\in\mathbb{R}
, and two control functors
\textup{{C}}_{Z}
and
\textup{{C}}_{X}
, we can still get a universal graphical language for
Qubit
with the following interpretation.

5.3
Control functor in general symmetric monoidal categories

Throughout the paper we focused on SMCs that are props. Nervertheless, the notion of control functor and its diagrammatic representation extends straightforwadly to general SMCs. The main difference is that a control functor is specific to a certain object. We generalise
Definition

1
as follows.

Definition 13

(control functors)
.

Given a SMC
C
, a
control structure
is a family of control functors
\textup{{C}}^{A}:\textbf{{C}}_{\textup{endo}}\to\textbf{{C}}_{\textup{endo}}
parametrized by objects
A\in\mathcal{O}(\textbf{{C}})
, mapping any object
B\in\mathcal{O}(\textbf{{C}})
to the object
A\otimes B
and any morphism
f:B\to B
to a morphism
\textup{{C}}^{A}(f):A\otimes B\to A\otimes B
while satisfying the coherence laws depicted in
Figure

6
.

Example 10
.

While
FdHilb
is not a prop, it is a SMC and the generalised notion of control functor applies.

The notion of points can also be extended to arbitrary SMCs. Moreover, if
\textup{{C}}^{A}
and
\textup{{C}}^{B}
have points (respectively denoted
\textup{{true}}_{A},\textup{{false}}_{A}
and
\textup{{true}}_{B},\textup{{false}}_{B}
), then
\textup{{true}}_{A}\otimes\textup{{true}}_{B}
and
\textup{{false}}_{A}\otimes\textup{{other}}_{B}
are points for
\textup{{C}}^{A\otimes B}
for any
\textup{{other}}_{B}:I\to B
, as well as
\textup{{true}}_{A}\otimes\textup{{true}}_{B}
and
\textup{{other}}_{A}\otimes\textup{{false}}_{B}
for any
\textup{{other}}_{A}:I\to A
.

6
Conclusion

In this paper, we have introduced controlled props as an extension of the prop formalism to capture control structures in diagrammatic reasoning.
Beyond quantum computing, we expect controlled props to be applicable in other domains where conditional behavior plays a central role, such as classical reversible computing or control theory. Future research could also investigate enriched variants of controlled props.

Appendix A
Sufficient condition for the conjugation law

In the following, given
n\in\mathbb{Z}
, the notation
[n]
denotes the set
\{i:i\in\mathbb{N},1\leq i\leq n\}
which contains all intergers between
1
and
n
(included). In particular, if
n\leq 0
then
[n]=\varnothing
.

Definition 14

(unitary dagger controlled prop)
.

A
unitary dagger controlled prop

P
is a dagger controlled prop containing only endomorphisms and such that
\textbf{{P}}\vdash f\circ f^{\dagger}=\textup{id}_{n}=f^{\dagger}\circ f
for any
f\in\textbf{{P}}(n,n)
.

Lemma 3
.

Given a unitary dagger controlled prop
P
,
\textbf{{P}}\vdash f=g
implies
\textbf{{P}}\vdash f^{\dagger}=g^{\dagger}
for any
f,g\in\textbf{{P}}(n,n)
.

Proof.

\textbf{{P}}\vdash f^{\dagger}=g^{\dagger}\circ g\circ f^{\dagger}=g^{\dagger}\circ f\circ f^{\dagger}=g^{\dagger}

∎

Definition 15

(reducibility)
.

Given a unitary dagger controlled prop
P
and a set
\mathcal{G}
of endomorphisms of
P
, let
\textbf{{P}}|_{\mathcal{G}}
be the subclass of morphisms inductively generated as follows.

\displaystyle f\in\textbf{{P}}|_{\mathcal{G}}(n,n)f:n\to n\in\mathcal{G}\hskip 50.00008pt(g\circ f)\in\textbf{{P}}|_{\mathcal{G}}(n,n)f,g\in\textbf{{P}}|_{\mathcal{G}}(n,n)\hskip 50.00008pt(f\otimes g)\in\textbf{{P}}|_{\mathcal{G}}(n+m,n+m)\lx@proof@logical@and f\in\textbf{{P}}|_{\mathcal{G}}(n,n)g\in\textbf{{P}}|_{\mathcal{G}}(m,m)

We say that
P
is
\mathcal{G}
-reducible if for any
f\in\textbf{{P}}(n,n)
there exists
f^{\prime}\in\textbf{{P}}|_{\mathcal{G}}(n,n)
such
\textbf{{P}}\vdash f=f^{\prime}
.

(sufficient condition)
.

\mathcal{G}
-reducible unitary dagger controlled prop
P
, the condition (

(
\star
)

where
f_{x,i}
and
g_{y,i}
are defined as follows for
x:n\to n,y:m\to m\in\mathcal{G}
and
i\in[n+m-1]
.

\displaystyle f_{x,i}=\textup{id}_{\max(0,i-n)}\otimes x\otimes\textup{id}_{\max(0,m-i)}\hskip 50.00008ptg_{y,i}=\textup{id}_{\max(0,n-i)}\otimes y\otimes\textup{id}_{\max(0,i-m)}

Proof.

Suppose that (

⋆

‣
4
), we prove the conjugation law (
23
) for arbitrary
f,g\in\textbf{{P}}(n,n)
.

As
P
is
\mathcal{G}
-reducible, any morphism in
\textbf{{P}}(n,n)
can be transformed into a morphism in
\textbf{{P}}|_{\mathcal{G}}(n,n)
.
Moreover, notice that the coherence laws of SMC (see
Figure

2
) ensure that for any
h\in\textbf{{P}}|_{\mathcal{G}}(n,n)
there exist
\ell\geq 1
and
p_{k},q_{k}\in\mathbb{N}
,
x_{k}:n_{k}\to n_{k}\in\mathcal{G}
satisfying
p_{k}+n_{k}+q_{k}=n
for all
1\leq k\leq\ell
, such that

\displaystyle\textbf{{P}}\vdash h=(\textup{id}_{p_{\ell}}\otimes x_{\ell}\otimes\textup{id}_{q_{\ell}})\circ(\textup{id}_{p_{\ell-1}}\otimes x_{\ell-1}\otimes\textup{id}_{q_{\ell-1}})\circ\dots\circ(\textup{id}_{p_{1}}\otimes x_{1}\otimes\textup{id}_{q_{1}})

Intuitively, we can transform any morphism
h
into a morphism
h^{\prime}
that is a sequential composition of
\ell
layers each containning a single morphism of
\mathcal{G}
sandwiched between identities.
Applied to
f
and
g
, this yields
f^{\prime}
and
g^{\prime}
of the above form such that

\textbf{{P}}\vdash f=f^{\prime}\hskip 30.00005pt\text{,}\hskip 30.00005pt\textbf{{P}}\vdash g=g^{\prime}\hskip 30.00005pt\text{and}\hskip 30.00005pt\textbf{{P}}\vdash g^{\dagger}=(g^{\prime})^{\dagger}

where the last equality is given by
Lemma

3
.
Then, proving the following equation is enough to conclude.

58

where the first induction hypothesis is applied for
(\ell_{g_{1}},\ell_{f}+2\ell_{g_{2}})<(\ell_{g},\ell_{f})
and the second induction hypothesis is applied for
(\ell_{g_{2}},\ell_{f})<(\ell_{g},\ell_{f})
.

The base cases
\ell_{f}=\ell_{g}=1
are the cases where
f^{\prime}
and
g^{\prime}
have a single layer. Denoting

f^{\prime}=(\textup{id}_{p}\otimes x\otimes\textup{id}_{q})\hskip 30.00005pt\text{and}\hskip 30.00005ptg^{\prime}=(\textup{id}_{r}\otimes y\otimes\textup{id}_{s})

where
p,q,r,s\in\mathbb{N}
and
x:n\to n,y:m\to m\in\mathcal{G}
. If
p\geq r+m
or
r\geq p+n
then
f^{\prime}
and
g^{\prime}
trivially commute (as well as
(\textup{id}_{1}\otimes g^{\prime})
and
\textup{{C}}(f^{\prime})
), and so the statement is straightforwardly proved using the fact that
P
is unitary. Otherwise, there exists a unique
i\in[n+m-1]
such that

\textbf{{P}}\vdash f^{\prime}=\textup{id}_{\min(p,r)}\otimes f_{x,i}\otimes\textup{id}_{\min(q,s)}\hskip 30.00005pt\text{and}\hskip 30.00005pt\textbf{{P}}\vdash g^{\prime}=\textup{id}_{\min(p,r)}\otimes g_{y,i}\otimes\textup{id}_{\min(q,s)}

Hence, we prove the bases cases as follows.

Proof.

Given a morphism
f\in\textbf{{CQC}}(n,n)
, we explain how to transform
f
into a morphism
f^{\prime}\in\textbf{{CQC}}|_{\mathcal{G}}(n,n)
. In the following, what we call a gate is either
\textup{id}_{n}
,
\sigma_{n,m}
,

\alpha

, or

H

.
Notice that all the
\sigma_{n,m}
gates can always be removed by applying
Equations

16
and
19
and then
Equation

38
.
Moreover, as
C
is a functor and
CQC
contains only endomorphisms, we can always apply
\textup{{C}}(g\circ f)=\textup{{C}}(g)\circ\textup{{C}}(f)
to split each control into multiple controlled gates.
Then, we iteratively reduce the number of controls of the remaining gates using
Equations

45
,
46
and
47
as well as their controlled versions (where
Equation

46
is only applied when
\alpha\neq\pi
to avoid infinite loops). The coherence laws ensure that this process can be applied to gates that are controlled by non adjacent wires, and we can remove the implicit
\sigma_{n,m}
gates that are hidden as explained above. At the end of this process, we get a morphism
f^{\prime}\in\textbf{{CQC}}|_{\mathcal{G}}(n,n)
.
∎

Lemma 6
.

\llbracket E(C)\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}=\llbracket C\rrbracket_{\textup{c}}
for any
C\in\textbf{{CQC}}|_{\mathcal{G}}(n,n)
.

Proof.

By structural induction with

\llbracket E(C_{1}\diamond C_{2})\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}=\llbracket E(C_{1})\diamond E(C_{2})\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}=\llbracket E(C_{1})\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}\diamond\llbracket E(C_{2})\rrbracket_{\textup{v}}\overset{\textup{IH}}{=}\llbracket C_{1}\rrbracket_{\textup{c}}\diamond\llbracket C_{2}\rrbracket_{\textup{c}}=\llbracket C_{1}\diamond C_{2}\rrbracket_{\textup{c}}

where
\diamond
is either
\circ
or
\otimes
, and where the base cases can be checked manually.
∎

Lemma 7
.

\textbf{{CQC}}\vdash D(\lambda^{n}(\alpha))=\mu^{n}(\alpha)
for any
n\in\mathbb{N}
and
\alpha\in\mathbb{R}
.

Proof.

By induction on
n
.
The base case where
n=0
or
n=1
are proved as follows.

\displaystyle D(\lambda^{0}(\alpha))=D(\!\scalebox{0.90}{{
\hbox to11.78pt{\vbox to11.78pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 5.89056pt\lower-5.89055pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \hbox to0.0pt{
{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} {{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{{}}{}{{{}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{{{}{}{}{}}}{{}{}{}{}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{{{}{}{}{}}}{{}{}{}{}}}}{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} {}\lxSVG@fillstroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 7.87 L 0 7.87 C 4.35 7.87 7.87 4.35 7.87 0 C 7.87 -4.35 4.35 -7.87 0 -7.87 L -0 -7.87 C -4.35 -7.87 -7.87 -4.35 -7.87 0 C -7.87 4.35 -4.35 7.87 -0 7.87 Z}{} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope }{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-3.1985pt}{-2.15277pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}

Lemma 8
.

If
\textbf{{QC}}\vdash C_{1}=C_{2}
then
\textbf{{CQC}}\vdash D(C_{1})=D(C_{2})
for any
C_{1},C_{2}\in\textbf{{QC}}(n,n)
.

C_{1}=C_{2}
in
\mathcal{R}_{\textup{vanilla}}

Lemma 9
.

\textbf{{CQC}}\vdash D(E(C))=C
for any
C\in\textbf{{CQC}}|_{\mathcal{G}}(n,n)
.

Proof.

D(E(C_{1}\diamond C_{2}))=D(E(C_{1})\diamond E(C_{2}))=D(E(C_{1}))\diamond D(E(C_{2}))\overset{\textup{IH}}{=}C_{1}\diamond C_{2}

where
\diamond
is either
\circ
or
\otimes
, and where the base cases are proved as follows.

Proof of
Theorem

2
.

Let
C_{1},C_{2}\in\textbf{{CQC}}(n,n)
such that
\llbracket C_{1}\rrbracket_{\textup{c}}=\llbracket C_{2}\rrbracket_{\textup{c}}
. By
Lemma

5
, there are some
C_{1}^{\prime},C_{2}^{\prime}\in\textbf{{CQC}}|_{\mathcal{G}}(n,n)
such that
\textbf{{CQC}}\vdash C_{i}=C_{i}^{\prime}
.
By
Lemma

6
and completeness of
QC
(see
Theorem

1
) we have
\textbf{{QC}}\vdash E(C_{1}^{\prime})=E(C_{2}^{\prime})
. Then, by
Lemma

8
,
\textbf{{CQC}}\vdash D(E(C_{1}^{\prime}))=D(E(C_{2}^{\prime}))
and
Lemma

9
concludes the proof as follows.

\textbf{{CQC}}\vdash C_{1}\hskip 8.00003pt\overset{\lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{lem:cqcreducing}}{=}\hskip 8.00003ptC_{1}^{\prime}\hskip 8.00003pt\overset{\lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{lem:decenc}}{=}\hskip 8.00003ptD(E(C_{1}^{\prime}))\hskip 8.00003pt\overset{\lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{lem:dec}}{=}\hskip 8.00003ptD(E(C_{2}^{\prime}))\hskip 8.00003pt\overset{\lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{lem:decenc}}{=}\hskip 8.00003ptC_{2}^{\prime}\hskip 8.00003pt\overset{\lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{lem:cqcreducing}}{=}\hskip 8.00003ptC_{2}

∎
